Bounds on the game isolation number and exact values for paths and cycles

Csilla Bujtás ††thanks: Supported by the Slovenian Research and Innovation Agency (ARIS) under the grants P1-0297, N1-0355, J1-70045.    Tanja Dravec ††thanks: Supported by the Slovenian Research and Innovation Agency (ARIS) under the grants P1-0297, N1-0431.    Michael A. Henning    Sandi Klavžar ††thanks: Supported by the Slovenian Research and Innovation Agency (ARIS) under the grants P1-0297, N1-0285, N1-0355, N1-0431, J1-70045. Faculty of Mathematics and Physics, University of Ljubljana, Ljubljana, Slovenia
Institute of Mathematics, Physics and Mechanics, Ljubljana, Slovenia
Faculty of Natural Sciences and Mathematics, University of Maribor, Maribor, Slovenia
Department of Mathematics and Applied Mathematics, University of Johannesburg, Johannesburg, South Africa
Abstract

The isolation game is played on a graph GG by two players who take turns playing a vertex such that if XX is the set of already played vertices, then a vertex can be selected only if it dominates a vertex from a nontrivial component of G∖NG​[X]G\setminus N_{G}[X], where NG​[X]N_{G}[X] is the set of vertices in XX or adjacent to a vertex in XX. Dominator wishes to finish the game with the minimum number of played vertices, while Staller has the opposite goal. The game isolation number ιg​(G)\iota_{\rm g}(G) is the number of moves in the Dominator-start game where both players play optimally. If Staller starts the game the invariant is denoted by ιg′​(G)\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(G). In this paper, ιg​(Cn)\iota_{\rm g}(C_{n}), ιg​(Pn)\iota_{\rm g}(P_{n}), ιg′​(Cn)\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(C_{n}), and ιg′​(Pn)\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(P_{n}) are determined for all nn. It is proved that there are only two graphs that attain equality in the upper bound ιg​(G)≤12​|V⁡(G)|\iota_{\rm g}(G)\leq\frac{1}{2}|V(G)|, and that there are precisely eleven graphs which attain equality in the upper bound ιg′​(G)≤12​|V⁡(G)|\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(G)\leq\frac{1}{2}|V(G)|. For trees TT of order at least three it is proved that ιg​(T)≤511​|V⁡(T)|\iota_{\rm g}(T)\leq\frac{5}{11}|V(T)|. A new infinite family of graphs GG is also constructed for which ιg​(G)=ιg′​(G)=37​|V⁡(G)|\iota_{\rm g}(G)=\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(G)=\frac{3}{7}|V(G)| holds.

Keywords: 
isolating set, isolation game, paths and cycles, trees

1 Introduction

Let G=(V⁡(G),E⁡(G))G=(V(G),E(G)) be a graph and let X⊆V⁡(G)X\subseteq V(G). The closed neighborhood of XX is defined as NG[X]=∪x∈XNG[x]N_{G}[X]=\cup_{x\in X}N_{G}[x], where NG​[x]N_{G}[x] is the closed neighborhood of xx in GG. We say that XX is an isolating set of GG if V​(G)∖NG​[X]V(G)\setminus N_{G}[X] is an independent set in GG. The minimum cardinality among all isolating sets in GG is the isolation number ι⁡(G)\iota(G) of GG. The concept was introduced (in a more general setting) in 2017 by Caro and Hansberg (2017). For an insight into current developments in the field, we recommend the following articles Borg (2025); Boyer and Goddard (2024); Boyer and Goddard (2025); Boyer et al. (2025); Chen et al. (2025); Lemańska et al. (2024); Zhang and Wu (2024a); Zhang and Wu (2024b) and references therein.

The domination game was introduced by Brešar et al. (2010). It was later extensively investigated, the summary of these researches up to 2021 is collected in the book of Brešar et al. (2021). Recent developments on the domination game include the papers by Bujtás et al. (2022); James and Vijayakumar (2023); Portier and Versteegen (2024); Versteegen (2024).

Moreover, several variations of the domination game were also investigated, notably the total domination game by Henning et al. (2015), the fractional domination game by Bujtás and Tuza (2019), the connected domination game by Borowiecki et al. (2019), two variants of the paired-domination game by Gray and Henning (2023); Haynes and Henning (2019), the competition-independence game of Phillips and Slater (2001), and the indicated domination game of Brešar et al. (2024).

More recently, Brešar et al. (2026) introduced a game counterpart of the isolation number following the ideas of the classical domination game (Brešar et al. (2010)). The isolation game is played on a graph GG by Dominator and Staller, who take turns selecting/playing a vertex from GG while obeying the rule that if XX is the set of already played vertices, then a vertex can be selected only if it dominates a vertex that belongs to a nontrivial component of the graph G−NG​[X]G-N_{G}[X]. Such a vertex xx is playable, and a move selecting xx is legal. The game ends when no playable vertex exists. When the game ends, the set of vertices selected forms an isolating set of GG. As in the domination game, Dominator wishes to finish the game by playing the fewest number of vertices, while Staller wishes to delay the process as much as possible. Thus, Dominator seeks to minimize the size of the chosen set while Staller tries to make it as large as possible. If Dominator starts the game, we speak of a D-game, otherwise it is an S-game. The game isolation number, ιg​(G)\iota_{\rm g}(G), and the Staller-start game isolation number, ιg′​(G)\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(G), are the number of vertices selected in the D-game and the S-game, respectively, provided that both players play optimally.

As mentioned above, the isolation number of a graph was introduced in a more general frame, the same holds for the isolation game defined by Brešar et al. (2026). A few results, such as the Continuation Principle and the fact that for each graph GG we have |ιg​(G)−ιg′​(G)|≤1|\iota_{\rm g}(G)-\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(G)|\leq 1, have been proved by Brešar et al. (2026) for the general situation, while a special focus has been given on the isolation game. It was proved that ιg​(G)\iota_{\rm g}(G) is at most half the order for any graph GG and conjectured that the actual sharp upper bound is the ceiling of three-sevenths of the order. The isolation number of paths PnP_{n} was also determined for the cases when n≡imod5n\equiv i\bmod 5, i∈{1,2,3}i\in\{1,2,3\}.

In Section 2, we determine the exact values for the (Staller-start) game isolation number for paths and cycles. Section 3 focuses on graphs whose game isolation number equals one half of their order. We first show that K2K_{2} and C6C_{6} are the only graphs that attain the bound ιg​(G)≤12​|V⁡(G)|\iota_{\rm g}(G)\leq\frac{1}{2}|V(G)|. We then prove that ιg′​(G)≤12​|V⁡(G)|\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(G)\leq\frac{1}{2}|V(G)| holds for every graph GG and identify all connected graphs for which equality holds. There are exactly eleven such graphs, all with order at most 10. In Section 4, we show that the 1/21/2-upper bound on the game isolation number in general graphs can be improved to 5/115/11 for trees. Regarding the 3/73/7-conjecture posed by Brešar et al. (2026), we present in Section 5 a new infinite family of graphs with minimum degree at least 2 that achieve this bound.

2 Game isolation number of paths and cycles

Brešar et al. (2026) established the following results on the game isolation number of paths.

Theorem 2.1.

(Brešar et al., 2026, Corollary 4.5) If n≥6n\geq 6, then

⌈2​n5⌉−1≤ιg​(Pn)≤ιg′​(Pn)≤⌊2​n+25⌋.\left\lceil\frac{2n}{5}\right\rceil-1\leq\iota_{\rm g}(P_{n})\leq\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(P_{n})\leq\left\lfloor\frac{2n+2}{5}\right\rfloor.
Theorem 2.2.

(Brešar et al., 2026, Corollary 4.6) Let n≥6n\geq 6. If nmod5∈{1,2,3}n\bmod 5\in\{1,2,3\}, then

ιg​(Pn)=ιg′​(Pn)=⌊2​n+25⌋.\iota_{\rm g}(P_{n})=\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(P_{n})=\left\lfloor\frac{2n+2}{5}\right\rfloor\,.

In the first main result of this section we determine the game isolation number for all cycles. After that, in our second main result we use some tools from the proof for cycles to round Theorems 2.1 and 2.2 by determining the exact values for all paths.

The result for cycles reads as follows.

Theorem 2.3.

For every n≥4n\geq 4,

ιg​(Cn)={2​⌈n5⌉;if ​n≡0mod5,2​⌈n5⌉−1;otherwise.\iota_{\rm g}(C_{n})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}2\left\lceil\frac{n}{5}\right\rceil;&\text{if~}n\equiv 0\bmod 5,\\ \\ 2\left\lceil\frac{n}{5}\right\rceil-1;&\text{otherwise}.\\ \end{array}\right.
ιg′​(Cn)={2​⌊n5⌋+1;if ​n≡4mod5,2​⌊n5⌋;otherwise.\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(C_{n})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}2\left\lfloor\frac{n}{5}\right\rfloor+1;&\text{if~}n\equiv 4\bmod 5,\\ \\ 2\left\lfloor\frac{n}{5}\right\rfloor;&\text{otherwise}.\\ \end{array}\right.
Proof.

For C4C_{4} and C5C_{5}, the formulas can be checked directly. In the continuation, we may assume n≥6n\geq 6 and prove lower and upper bounds on the invariants by observing strategies for Staller and Dominator, respectively in the subsequent two claims.

Claim 2.3.1.

For every n≥6n\geq 6,

min⁡{2​⌈n5⌉,2​⌈n−45⌉+1}≤ιg​(Cn)\min\left\{2\left\lceil\frac{n}{5}\right\rceil,2\left\lceil\frac{n-4}{5}\right\rceil+1\right\}\leq\iota_{\rm g}(C_{n}) (1)

and

min⁡{2​⌈n−35⌉,2​⌈n−45⌉+1}≤ιg′​(Cn).\min\left\{2\left\lceil\frac{n-3}{5}\right\rceil,2\left\lceil\frac{n-4}{5}\right\rceil+1\right\}\leq\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(C_{n}). (2)
Proof.

We consider the following strategy of Staller. In each of her moves, she plays a (playable) vertex that is a neighbor of an already played vertex. Observe that it is always possible when the game is not over. By a run BiB_{i} we mean a maximal sequence of played vertices along the cycle. Let B1,…,BℓB_{1},\dots,B_{\ell} be the runs obtained when the game is over. According to Staller’s strategy, she never increases the number of runs except in the first move in the S-game. Hence, the number of Dominator’s moves is an upper bound on ℓ\ell and ℓ−1\ell-1 in the D-game and S-game, respectively. Between any two consecutive runs there are at most three unplayed vertices. Let t=∑i=1ℓ|Bi|,t=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}|B_{i}|, which is exactly the number of played vertices during the game.

We first prove (1) and assume that a D-game is played on CnC_{n}. If tt is even, Staller finishes the game and the number of runs can be estimated as ℓ≤t/2\ell\leq t/2. Therefore,

n≤t+3​t2=5​t2n\leq t+3\,\frac{t}{2}=5\,\frac{t}{2}

and, as t2\frac{t}{2} is an integer, we have t2≥⌈n5⌉.\frac{t}{2}\geq\left\lceil\frac{n}{5}\right\rceil. Hence we may conclude 2​⌈n5⌉≤t2\left\lceil\frac{n}{5}\right\rceil\leq t when tt is even. If tt is odd, then Dominator plays t+12\frac{t+1}{2} vertices and ℓ≤t+12.\ell\leq\frac{t+1}{2}. This implies

n≤t+3​t+12=5​t−12+4.n\leq t+3\,\frac{t+1}{2}=5\,\frac{t-1}{2}+4.

Since t−12\frac{t-1}{2} is an integer, we get 2​⌈n−45⌉+1≤t2\left\lceil\frac{n-4}{5}\right\rceil+1\leq t for the case of tt is odd. Putting together the cases with odd and even tt, we obtain inequality (1).

For the SS-game, we can prove (2) in an analogous way. Here, the first move of Staller creates a new run, but later she does not increase the number of runs. Hence, the number of Dominator’s moves is an upper bound on ℓ−1\ell-1. If tt, the number of played vertices, is an even number, then ℓ≤t2+1\ell\leq\frac{t}{2}+1 and

n≤t+3​(t2+1)=5​t2+3.n\leq t+3\left(\frac{t}{2}+1\right)=5\,\frac{t}{2}+3.

Therefore, 2​⌈n−35⌉≤t2\left\lceil\frac{n-3}{5}\right\rceil\leq t holds if tt is even. If tt is odd, then Staller finishes the game, and we get

n≤t+3​(t−12+1)=5​t−12+4n\leq t+3\left(\frac{t-1}{2}+1\right)=5\,\frac{t-1}{2}+4

and conclude 2​⌈n−45⌉+1≤t.2\left\lceil\frac{n-4}{5}\right\rceil+1\leq t. From the odd and even cases, we get (2) as stated. (□\Box)

Claim 2.3.2.

For every n≥6n\geq 6, the following inequalities hold.

  1. (a)

    If n≢0mod5n\not\equiv 0\bmod{5}, then ιg​(Cn)≤2​⌈n5⌉−1\iota_{\rm g}(C_{n})\leq 2\left\lceil\frac{n}{5}\right\rceil-1. If n≡0mod5n\equiv 0\bmod{5}, then ιg​(Cn)≤2​⌈n5⌉\iota_{\rm g}(C_{n})\leq 2\left\lceil\frac{n}{5}\right\rceil.

  2. (b)

    If n≢4mod5n\not\equiv 4\bmod{5}, then ιg′​(Cn)≤2​⌊n5⌋\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(C_{n})\leq 2\left\lfloor\frac{n}{5}\right\rfloor. If n≡4mod5n\equiv 4\bmod{5}, then ιg′​(Cn)≤2​⌊n5⌋+1\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(C_{n})\leq 2\left\lfloor\frac{n}{5}\right\rfloor+1.

Proof.

To prove the upper bounds stated in the claim, we consider the following strategy of Dominator. If it is not the first move in the game, then Dominator chooses a vertex viv_{i} such that vi−4v_{i-4} is a played vertex and vi−3,vi−2,vi−1v_{i-3},v_{i-2},v_{i-1} are all unplayed. If the game is not over, then he is able to follow this strategy. We further note that if there is a playable vertex vjv_{j} in CnC_{n} (at any moment in the game), then there is a sequence of at least four consecutive playable vertices that includes vjv_{j}. Consequently, if CnC_{n} contains at most seven playable vertices before a move of Dominator, then these vertices form a sequence, and Dominator can choose one of them to finish the game with this move. If the number of playable vertices is eight, then Dominator can follow his strategy, which ensures that the next move played by Staller will finish the game. For both the D-game and S-game, we count the playable and unplayable vertices after each move in CnC_{n} to prove the upper bounds. Let uiu_{i} denote the number of vertices made unplayable by the ithi^{\rm th} move in the game.

(a) Assume that a D-game is played. The first move of Dominator makes exactly one vertex (the played vertex itself) unplayable, u1=1u_{1}=1. Then, for Staller’s move, we have u2≥1u_{2}\geq 1. As Dominator’s strategy ensures, his every later move makes at least four vertices unplayable and hence u2​j−1≥4u_{2j-1}\geq 4 for every j≥2j\geq 2. For Staller’s moves, we have u2​j≥1u_{2j}\geq 1. In general, there are

U2​i=∑s=12​ius≥2+5​(i−1)=5​i−3U_{2i}=\sum_{s=1}^{2i}u_{s}\geq 2+5(i-1)=5i-3

unplayable vertices after 2​i2i moves in the game.

  • •

    If n=5​kn=5k, then U2​k−2≥5​k−8U_{2k-2}\geq 5k-8 and at most eight playable vertices remain before Dominator’s move. He can make sure that the game finishes with the (2​k)th(2k)^{\rm th} move or sooner. Therefore, ιg​(Cn)≤2​k=2​⌈n5⌉\iota_{\rm g}(C_{n})\leq 2k=2\left\lceil\frac{n}{5}\right\rceil as stated.

  • •

    If n=5​k+rn=5k+r with r∈{1,…,4}r\in\{1,\dots,4\}, then U2​k≥5​k−3U_{2k}\geq 5k-3 implies that at most r+3≤7r+3\leq 7 vertices are playable before Dominator’s move and he can end the game with the (2​k+1)st(2k+1)^{\rm st} move (if it was not finished earlier). Therefore, ιg​(Cn)≤2​k+1=2​⌈n5⌉−1.\iota_{\rm g}(C_{n})\leq 2k+1=2\left\lceil\frac{n}{5}\right\rceil-1.

(b) In an S-game on CnC_{n} Dominator’s strategy implies u1=1u_{1}=1, u2≥4u_{2}\geq 4, and in general, u2​j−1≥1u_{2j-1}\geq 1 and u2​j≥4u_{2j}\geq 4. After 2​i−12i-1 moves, the number of unplayable vertices, U2​i−1U_{2i-1}, is at least 5​i−45i-4.

  • •

    If n=5​k+4n=5k+4, then U2​k−1≥5​k−4U_{2k-1}\geq 5k-4. Thus, at most eight playable vertices remain and the game finishes with the (2​k+1)st(2k+1)^{\rm st} move or sooner. We conclude that ιg′​(Cn)≤2​k+1=2​⌊n5⌋+1\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(C_{n})\leq 2k+1=2\left\lfloor\frac{n}{5}\right\rfloor+1.

  • •

    If n=5​k+rn=5k+r with r∈{0,…,3}r\in\{0,\dots,3\}, then U2​k−1≥5​k−4U_{2k-1}\geq 5k-4 implies that the number of playable vertices is at most 4+r≤74+r\leq 7. It follows that Dominator can finish the game with his next move and ιg′​(Cn)≤2​k=2​⌊n5⌋.\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(C_{n})\leq 2k=2\left\lfloor\frac{n}{5}\right\rfloor. (□\Box)

To complete the proof of the theorem, we compare the lower and upper bounds in Claims 2.3.1 and 2.3.2.

If n=5​kn=5k, then

2​⌈n5⌉=2​k<2​k+1=2​⌈n−45⌉+1,2\left\lceil\frac{n}{5}\right\rceil=2k<2k+1=2\left\lceil\frac{n-4}{5}\right\rceil+1,

and (1) gives 2​⌈n5⌉≤ιg​(Cn).2\left\lceil\frac{n}{5}\right\rceil\leq\iota_{\rm g}(C_{n}). Then, the upper bound in Claim 2.3.2(a) gives the desired equality. If n=5​k+rn=5k+r with r∈{1,…,4}r\in\{1,\dots,4\}, then

2​⌈n5⌉=2​k+2>2​k+1=2​⌈n−45⌉+1,2\left\lceil\frac{n}{5}\right\rceil=2k+2>2k+1=2\left\lceil\frac{n-4}{5}\right\rceil+1,

and (1) implies 2​k+1≤ιg​(Cn)2k+1\leq\iota_{\rm g}(C_{n}). On the other hand, Claim 2.3.2(a) establishes ιg​(Cn)≤2​⌈n5⌉−1=2​k+1.\iota_{\rm g}(C_{n})\leq 2\left\lceil\frac{n}{5}\right\rceil-1=2k+1. We may therefore infer ιg​(Cn)=2​⌈n5⌉−1.\iota_{\rm g}(C_{n})=2\left\lceil\frac{n}{5}\right\rceil-1.

For ιg′​(Cn)\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(C_{n}), we first consider the case of n=5​k+4n=5k+4 and observe

2​⌈n−35⌉=2​k+2>2​k+1=2​⌈n−45⌉+1.2\left\lceil\frac{n-3}{5}\right\rceil=2k+2>2k+1=2\left\lceil\frac{n-4}{5}\right\rceil+1.

Inequality (2) then yields 2​k+1≤ιg′​(Cn)2k+1\leq\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(C_{n}) which matches the upper bound in Claim 2.3.2(b) and proves ιg′​(Cn)=2​⌊n5⌋+1.\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(C_{n})=2\left\lfloor\frac{n}{5}\right\rfloor+1. If n=5​k+rn=5k+r with r∈{0,…,3}r\in\{0,\dots,3\}, then

2​⌈n−35⌉=2​k<2​k+1=2​⌈n−45⌉+12\left\lceil\frac{n-3}{5}\right\rceil=2k<2k+1=2\left\lceil\frac{n-4}{5}\right\rceil+1

and (2) gives 2​k≤ιg′​(Cn)2k\leq\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(C_{n}). By Claim 2.3.2(b) we know that ιg′​(Cn)≤2​k=2​⌊n5⌋.\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(C_{n})\leq 2k=2\left\lfloor\frac{n}{5}\right\rfloor. This finishes the proof of the theorem. ∎

We now complete Theorems 2.1 and 2.2 by establishing the exact values of ιg​(Pn)\iota_{\rm g}(P_{n}) and ιg′​(Pn)\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(P_{n}) when n≡0mod5n\equiv 0\bmod 5, and n≡4mod5n\equiv 4\bmod 5.

Theorem 2.4.

Let n≥6n\geq 6. If n≡0mod5n\equiv 0\bmod 5, or n≡4mod5n\equiv 4\bmod 5, then

ιg​(Pn)=⌈2​n5⌉−1andιg′​(Pn)=⌊2​n+25⌋.\iota_{\rm g}(P_{n})=\left\lceil\frac{2n}{5}\right\rceil-1\qquad{\rm and}\qquad\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(P_{n})=\left\lfloor\frac{2n+2}{5}\right\rfloor.
Proof.

We first prove that the lower bound ⌈2​n5⌉−1≤ιg​(Pn)\left\lceil\frac{2n}{5}\right\rceil-1\leq\iota_{\rm g}(P_{n}) in Theorem 2.1 is tight when n=5​kn=5k or n=5​k+4n=5k+4. Consider a D-game on Pn:v1​…​vnP_{n}\colon v_{1}\dots v_{n} when Dominator applies the strategy described in the proof of Theorem 2.3, Claim 2.3.2. More exactly, Dominator plays v3v_{3} as his first move, and later he chooses to play a vertex viv_{i} such that vi−4v_{i-4} is played and vi−3,vi−2,vi−1,viv_{i-3},v_{i-2},v_{i-1},v_{i} are all unplayed. If there is no such vertex viv_{i}, then either the game is over or the last three vertices of the path are unplayed, and the only edge which is not isolated is vn−1​vnv_{n-1}v_{n}. Let tt denote the number of moves in this game.

Let uju_{j} denote the number of vertices made unplayable by the jthj^{\rm th} move of the game and let Uj=∑s=1jusU_{j}=\sum_{s=1}^{j}u_{s} be the total number of unplayable vertices after the jthj^{\rm th} move. By Dominator’s strategy, u1≥3u_{1}\geq 3, and u2​j−1≥4u_{2j-1}\geq 4 for every j≥2j\geq 2 if t>2​j−1t>2j-1. Therefore, U2​j≥5​j−1U_{2j}\geq 5j-1 holds if t>2​jt>2j.

If n=5​kn=5k, then U2​k−2≥5​k−6.U_{2k-2}\geq 5k-6. Hence, after 2​k−22k-2 moves in the game, at most six vertices are playable. Then these six vertices must be consecutive on the path, and Dominator can finish the game with his next move. It gives ιg​(Pn)≤t≤2​k−1=⌈2​n5⌉−1\iota_{\rm g}(P_{n})\leq t\leq 2k-1=\left\lceil\frac{2n}{5}\right\rceil-1 and proves the formula for n=5​kn=5k. If n=5​k+4n=5k+4, then we can give a similar reasoning. In this case, U2​k≥5​k−1U_{2k}\geq 5k-1 that is, at most five vertices are playable after 2​k2k moves. These are consecutive vertices, and Dominator can finish the game with his next move. We may conclude ιg​(Pn)≤t≤2​k+1=⌈2​n5⌉−1\iota_{\rm g}(P_{n})\leq t\leq 2k+1=\left\lceil\frac{2n}{5}\right\rceil-1 and equality follows by Theorem 2.1.

Consider now an S-game on PnP_{n}. To prove a lower bound on ιg′​(Pn)\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(P_{n}), we suppose that Staller plays according to the strategy described in the proof of Theorem 2.3, Claim 2.3.1. Her first move is v1v_{1}, and later she always plays a vertex next to an already played vertex. By this strategy, if ℓ\ell is the number of runs (maximal sequences of consecutive played vertices) at the end of the game, then Dominator played at least ℓ−1\ell-1 vertices. Recall also that there are at most three unplayed vertices between two consecutive runs. By Staller’s strategy, v1v_{1} belongs to a run. At the other end of the path, at most two unplayed vertices may remain. Again, let tt denote the number of moves in the game.

If tt is even, then Dominator played t/2t/2 vertices and

n≤t+3​ℓ−1≤t+3​(t2+1)−1=5​t2+2.n\leq t+3\ell-1\leq t+3\left(\frac{t}{2}+1\right)-1=5\,\frac{t}{2}+2.

Since t2\frac{t}{2} is an integer, it is equivalent to 2​⌈n−25⌉≤t.2\left\lceil\frac{n-2}{5}\right\rceil\leq t. If tt is odd, then Dominator played (t−1)/2(t-1)/2 vertices and

n≤t+3​ℓ−1≤t+3​(t−12+1)−1=5​t−12+3n\leq t+3\ell-1\leq t+3\left(\frac{t-1}{2}+1\right)-1=5\,\frac{t-1}{2}+3

follows. Hence we get 2​⌈n−35⌉+1≤t.2\left\lceil\frac{n-3}{5}\right\rceil+1\leq t. From the two cases, we derive

m=min⁡{2​⌈n−25⌉,2​⌈n−35⌉+1}≤t≤ιg′​(Pn).m=\min\left\{2\left\lceil\frac{n-2}{5}\right\rceil,2\left\lceil\frac{n-3}{5}\right\rceil+1\right\}\leq t\leq\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(P_{n}). (3)

Finally, we compare (3) with the upper bound ιg′​(Pn)≤⌊2​n+25⌋\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(P_{n})\leq\left\lfloor\frac{2n+2}{5}\right\rfloor from Theorem 2.1. If n=5​kn=5k, then m=2​km=2k, and it equals the upper bound. If n=5​k+4n=5k+4, then m=2​k+2m=2k+2, which matches the upper bound again. We conclude that ιg′​(Pn)=⌊2​n+25⌋\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(P_{n})=\left\lfloor\frac{2n+2}{5}\right\rfloor holds in both cases as stated. ∎

Combining Theorems 2.4 and 2.2 and verifying the formulas directly for n∈{1,…,5}n\in\{1,\dots,5\}, the complete result for paths can be stated as follows.

Theorem 2.5.

For every n≥1n\geq 1, we have

ιg​(Pn)={⌊2​n+15⌋−1;if ​n≡0mod5,⌊2​n+15⌋;otherwise,\iota_{\rm g}(P_{n})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\left\lfloor\frac{2n+1}{5}\right\rfloor-1;&\text{if~}n\equiv 0\bmod{5},\\ \\ \left\lfloor\frac{2n+1}{5}\right\rfloor;&\text{otherwise},\\ \end{array}\right.

and

ιg′​(Pn)=⌊2​n+25⌋.\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(P_{n})=\left\lfloor\frac{2n+2}{5}\right\rfloor.

3 Graphs that attain the 1/2-bound

It was proved by Brešar et al. (2026) that the game isolation number of a graph is at most one-half its order. We characterize the graphs achieving equality in this upper bound on the game isolation number. For this purpose, we follow the proof technique employed in Brešar et al. (2026), with the modification that we adopt a greedy strategy for Dominator.

For completeness, we include the key strategy of the proof in Brešar et al. (2026). During the course of the game, when SS is the set of selected vertices, a vertex vv is considered marked if v∈NG​[S]v\in N_{G}[S] or if all neighbors of vv are in NG​[S]N_{G}[S]. Note that a marked vertex may or may not be playable and a vertex is not playable if and only if its entire closed neighborhood is marked.

Theorem 3.1.

If GG is a connected graph of order nn, then ιg​(G)≤12​n\iota_{\rm g}(G)\leq\frac{1}{2}n, with equality if and only if G∈{K2,C6}G\in\{K_{2},C_{6}\}.

Proof.

Let GG be a connected graph of order nn. If n=1n=1, then ιg​(G)=0\iota_{\rm g}(G)=0, while if n=2n=2, then G=K2G=K_{2} and ιg​(G)=1=12​n\iota_{\rm g}(G)=1=\frac{1}{2}n. Hence we may assume that n≥3n\geq 3, for otherwise the desired result is immediate. Following the proof strategy employed in Brešar et al. (2026), we weight the vertices in the graph GG as follows. At the beginning all vertices are unmarked and each vertex has weight 11. During the game, when a vertex is marked its weight drops to 00. The weight w⁡(G){\rm w}(G) of GG is the sum of weights of all vertices of GG. Thus at the beginning of the game w⁡(G)=n{\rm w}(G)=n and when the game ends the weight is zero. Let MM be the set of marked vertices in some stage of the game.

We adopt a refinement of Dominator’s strategy as given in Brešar et al. (2026) in that Dominator now adopts a greedy strategy and plays a vertex that results in a maximum weight decrease. At the start of the game, Dominator therefore plays a vertex of maximum degree Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G), thereby marking at least Δ⁡(G)+1\Delta(G)+1 vertices and decreasing the weight by at least Δ⁡(G)+1\Delta(G)+1 on his first move. On each of his subsequent moves, if there exists a component CC of G−MG-M of order at least 33, then Dominator can always decrease the weight by at least 33 by playing a vertex of degree at least 22 in CC. Every move of Staller decreases the weight of GG by at least 11 since she must dominate at least one (unmarked) vertex in G−MG-M.

In the final stage of the game when every component in G−MG-M is a K2K_{2}-component, every move decreases the weight by at least 22. By playing a vertex in a K2K_{2}-component of G−MG-M, we note that Staller can play a move that decreases the weight by exactly 22. However according to Dominator’s greedy strategy, he plays a marked vertex that is adjacent to the maximum number of K2K_{2}-components in G−MG-M, thereby decreasing the weight by at least 22.

In summary, Dominator’s greedy strategy implies all his moves decrease the weight by at least 33, except possibly in the final stage of the game when every component in G−MG-M is a K2K_{2}-component, in which case all his subsequent moves decrease the weight by at least 22 and all subsequent moves of Staller decrease the weight by exactly 22. Moreover if at least one component of G−MG-M is of order at least 33, then Staller’s move decreases the weight of GG by at least 11. Hence every move of Dominator decreases the weight by at least 22, while each of Dominator’s move together with Staller’s reply to his move decrease the weight by at least 44. Therefore on average every played move decreases the weight by at least 22, implying that the game finishes after at most 12​n\frac{1}{2}n moves.

By our earlier assumption, recall that n≥3n\geq 3, and so Δ⁡(G)≥2\Delta(G)\geq 2. Suppose that Δ⁡(G)≥3\Delta(G)\geq 3. In this case, Dominator’s first move decreases the weight by at least 44. Since Staller’s move decreases the weight by at least 11, after the first two moves are played at least five vertices are marked. Thereafter, Dominator’s greedy strategy guarantees that at most 12​(n−5)\frac{1}{2}(n-5) additional moves are needed to finish the game. Hence in this case the game finishes after at most 2+12​(n−5)=12​(n−1)2+\frac{1}{2}(n-5)=\frac{1}{2}(n-1) moves, and so ιg​(G)<12​n\iota_{\rm g}(G)<\frac{1}{2}n.

Hence we may assume that Δ⁡(G)=2\Delta(G)=2. Thus, GG is a path PnP_{n} or a cycle CnC_{n}. Suppose that G=PnG=P_{n} (and n≥3n\geq 3). Then by Theorem 2.5, we have ιg​(G)≤25​(n+1)<12​n.\iota_{\rm g}(G)\leq\frac{2}{5}(n+1)<\frac{1}{2}n. Hence if G=PnG=P_{n} and n≥3n\geq 3, then ιg​(G)<12​n\iota_{\rm g}(G)<\frac{1}{2}n.

Suppose finally that G=CnG=C_{n}. If n∈{3,4}n\in\{3,4\}, then ιg​(G)=1<12​n\iota_{\rm g}(G)=1<\frac{1}{2}n. If n=5n=5, then ιg​(G)=2<12​n\iota_{\rm g}(G)=2<\frac{1}{2}n. If n=6n=6, then ιg​(G)=3=12​n\iota_{\rm g}(G)=3=\frac{1}{2}n. Hence we may assume that n≥7n\geq 7. By Theorem 2.3, we now infer the following. If n≡0mod5n\equiv 0\bmod{5}, then ιg​(Cn)=25​n<12​n.\iota_{\rm g}(C_{n})=\frac{2}{5}n<\frac{1}{2}n. If n≡1mod5n\equiv 1\bmod{5}, then ιg​(Cn)=25​(n+4)−1<12​n.\iota_{\rm g}(C_{n})=\frac{2}{5}(n+4)-1<\frac{1}{2}n. If n≡2mod5n\equiv 2\bmod{5}, then ιg​(Cn)=25​(n+3)−1<12​n.\iota_{\rm g}(C_{n})=\frac{2}{5}(n+3)-1<\frac{1}{2}n. If n≡3mod5n\equiv 3\bmod{5}, then ιg​(Cn)=25​(n+2)−1<12​n.\iota_{\rm g}(C_{n})=\frac{2}{5}(n+2)-1<\frac{1}{2}n. If n≡4mod5n\equiv 4\bmod{5}, then ιg​(Cn)=25​(n+1)−1<12​n.\iota_{\rm g}(C_{n})=\frac{2}{5}(n+1)-1<\frac{1}{2}n. In all cases, when n≥7n\geq 7 we have ιg​(Cn)<12​n\iota_{\rm g}(C_{n})<\frac{1}{2}n. Hence we have shown that G=K2G=K_{2} and G=C6G=C_{6} are the only graphs that satisfy ιg​(Cn)=12​n\iota_{\rm g}(C_{n})=\frac{1}{2}n. ∎

We prove next that the Staller-start game isolation number of a graph is at most one-half its order, and we characterize the graphs achieving equality in the 12​n\frac{1}{2}n-upper bound on the Staller-start game isolation number. For this purpose, let ℱ={F1,F2,…,F11}{\cal F}=\{F_{1},F_{2},\ldots,F_{11}\} be the family of eleven graphs illustrated in Fig. 1.

Theorem 3.2.

If GG is a connected graph of order nn, then ιg′​(G)≤12​n\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(G)\leq\frac{1}{2}n, with equality if and only if G∈ℱG\in{\cal F}.

Proof.

Let GG be a connected graph of order nn. We first prove the desired upper bound.

Claim 3.2.1.

ιg′​(G)≤12​n\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(G)\leq\frac{1}{2}n.

Proof.

If n=1n=1, then ιg′​(G)=0\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(G)=0, hence assume in the rest that n≥2n\geq 2. As in the proof of Theorem 3.1, we show that if Dominator employs his greedy strategy, then the game finishes after at most 12​n\frac{1}{2}n moves. Also, let MM be the set of marked vertices in some stage of the game. At the start of the game, Staller plays a vertex that marks at least δ⁡(G)+1\delta(G)+1 vertices. Therefore her first move decreases the weight by at least 22. Thereafter, as shown in the proof of Theorem 3.1, Staller’s subsequent moves decrease the weight by at least 11. Moreover in the final stage of the game when every component in G−MG-M is a K2K_{2}-component, every move of Staller decreases the weight by at least 22. As shown in the proof of Theorem 3.1, Dominator has a strategy that guarantees that all his moves decrease the weight by at least 33, except possibly in the final stage of the game when every component in G−MG-M is a K2K_{2}-component, in which case all his subsequent moves decrease the weight by at least 22.

If Dominator’s first move decreases the weight by exactly 22, then since he follows the greedy strategy, all moves played in the game decrease the weight by exactly 22, implying that the game finishes after 12​n\frac{1}{2}n moves. Hence we may assume that the first move of Dominator decreases the weight by at least 33, for otherwise the desired upper bound follows. Let i+1i+1 be the first move of Dominator that decreases the weight by exactly 22, where i≥1i\geq 1. Thus, all moves after Dominator plays his (i+1)(i+1)th move decrease the weight by exactly 22. The first move of Staller decreases the weight by at least 22, while all her other moves played before Dominator’s (i+1)(i+1)th move decrease the weight by at least 11. Hence the first 2​i+12i+1 moves played in the game (that is, all moves played immediately before Dominator plays his (i+1)(i+1)th move) decrease the total weight by at least 2+i+3​i=2​(2​i+1)2+i+3i=2(2i+1). Thus on average every played move decreases the weight by at least 22, implying that the game finishes after at most 12​n\frac{1}{2}n moves. This establishes the desired upper bound, namely ιg′​(G)≤12​n\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(G)\leq\frac{1}{2}n. (□\Box)

Suppose next that ιg′​(G)=12​n\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(G)=\frac{1}{2}n. In particular, n≥2n\geq 2 is even. If n∈{2,4}n\in\{2,4\}, then it is straightforward to verify that in this case G∈{F1,F2,F3}G\in\{F_{1},F_{2},F_{3}\}. Hence we may assume that in the rest of the proof n≥6n\geq 6. We proceed further with a series of claims establishing some structural properties of the graph GG.

Claim 3.2.2.

Staller’s first move decreases the weight by exactly 22.

Proof.

Suppose that Staller’s first move decreases the weight by at least 33. As observed earlier, on average every move played after the first move of Staller decreases the weight by at least 22, implying that the game finishes after at most 1+12​(n−3)<12​n1+\frac{1}{2}(n-3)<\frac{1}{2}n moves, a contradiction. (□\Box)

By Claim 3.2.2, Staller’s first move decreases the weight by exactly 22, implying that the first move of Staller is a vertex of degree 11. Let uu be the vertex played by Staller on her first move, and let vv be the (unique) neighbor of uu in GG. Thus at this opening stage of the game, we have M={u,v}M=\{u,v\}.

Claim 3.2.3.

Every move of Dominator decreases the weight by 22 or 33.

Proof.

Suppose that after the first move of Staller, every component of G−MG-M is a K2K_{2}-component. By assumption n≥6n\geq 6, and so G−MG-M contains k≥2k\geq 2 components and n=2​k+2n=2k+2. Dominator now plays the vertex vv as his first move, thereby marking all vertices, and so ιg′​(G)=2<k+1=12​n,\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(G)=2<k+1=\frac{1}{2}n, a contradiction. Hence, at least one component of G−MG-M has order at least 33. The first move of Dominator therefore decreases the weight by at least 33.

Suppose that the first move of Dominator decreases the weight by at least 44. The second move of Staller decreases the weight by at least 11. Hence after the first three moves of the game (that is, after Staller’s first and second move and Dominator’s first move) at least 2+4+1=72+4+1=7 vertices are marked. Thereafter, on average every move played starting with the second move of Dominator decreases the weight by at least 22, implying that the game finishes after at most 3+12​(n−7)<12​n3+\frac{1}{2}(n-7)<\frac{1}{2}n moves, a contradiction. Hence, the first move of Dominator decreases the weight by exactly 33. Analogous argument shows that if Dominator plays a move that decreases the weight by at least 44 at any stage in the game, then the game finishes after strictly less than 12​n\frac{1}{2}n moves, a contradiction. Hence, every move of Dominator decreases the weight by 22 or 33. (□\Box)

Let UU denote the set of unmarked vertices, and so U=V⁡(G)∖M.U=V(G)\setminus M.

Claim 3.2.4.

At any stage after Staller’s first move, the following properties hold.

  1. (a)

    Every vertex in MM has at most three neighbors in UU.

  2. (b)

    Every vertex in UU has at most two neighbors in UU.

  3. (c)

    G−MG-M is the disjoint union of paths and cycles.

  4. (d)

    If it is Dominator’s move and G−MG-M contains a path component, then such a component is a P2P_{2}- or P3P_{3}-component.

Proof.

If it is Dominator’s move and there is vertex in MM with four or more neighbors in UU, then Dominator can play such a vertex and decrease the weight by at least 44, contradicting Claim 3.2.3. Hence if it is Dominator’s move, then every vertex in MM has at most three neighbors in UU.

If it is Dominator’s move and there is a vertex in UU with three or more neighbors in UU, then Dominator can play such a vertex and decrease the weight by at least 44, contradicting Claim 3.2.3. Hence if it is Dominator’s move, then every vertex in UU has at most two neighbors in UU.

Immediately after Staller plays her first move, namely the vertex uu, we have M={u,v}M=\{u,v\}. At this opening stage of the game (M={u,v}M=\{u,v\}), properties (a) and (b) in the statement of Claim 3.2.4 hold. Since properties (a) and (b) are preserved as the game progresses, we infer that properties (a) and (b) also hold if it is Staller’s move. This proves Parts (a) and (b).

By Part (b), G−MG-M has maximum degree at most 22 and is therefore the disjoint union of paths and cycles. This proves Part (c).

Suppose that it is Dominator’s move and that G−MG-M contains a path component P:v1​v2​…​vpP\colon v_{1}v_{2}\ldots v_{p}, where p≥4p\geq 4. In this case, if Dominator plays the vertex v3v_{3}, then he marks at least v1v_{1}, v2v_{2}, v3v_{3}, and v4v_{4}, and therefore decreases the weight by at least 44, contradicting Claim 3.2.3. This proves Part (d). (□\Box)

We now return to the opening stage of the game, that is, immediately after Staller plays her first move, namely the vertex uu, and so M={u,v}M=\{u,v\}. Let G1,…,GkG_{1},\ldots,G_{k} denote the components of G−MG-M. By Claim 3.2.4(a), the vertex v∈Mv\in M is adjacent to at most three vertices in U=V⁡(G)∖{u,v},U=V(G)\setminus\{u,v\}, and so k≤3k\leq 3. By Claim 3.2.4(c), every component GiG_{i} is a path or cycle.

Claim 3.2.5.

In the initial stage of the game when M={u,v}M=\{u,v\}, no component of G−MG-M is a C4C_{4}-component.

Proof.

Suppose that immediately after Staller’s first move, there exists a C4C_{4}-component C:v1​v2​v3​v4​v1C\colon v_{1}v_{2}v_{3}v_{4}v_{1} in G−MG-M where v​v1∈E⁡(G)vv_{1}\in E(G). In this case, if Dominator plays the vertex v1v_{1}, then he marks all four vertices in the component CC. Hence, Dominator can decrease the weight by at least 44, contradicting Claim 3.2.3. (□\Box)

Claim 3.2.6.

In the initial stage of the game when M={u,v}M=\{u,v\}, if G−MG-M contains a path component, then such a component is a P3P_{3}-component.

Proof.

Suppose that immediately after Staller’s first move, there exists a path component P:v1​v2​…​vpP\colon v_{1}v_{2}\ldots v_{p} in G−MG-M for some p≥2p\geq 2. By Claim 3.2.4(d), we infer that p∈{2,3}p\in\{2,3\}. More generally, every path component in G−MG-M is a P2P_{2}- or P3P_{3}-component.

We show that p=3p=3. Suppose, to the contrary, that p=2p=2. Renaming components of G−MG-M, we may assume that G1=PG_{1}=P, and so G1G_{1} is a P2P_{2}-component. We may further assume that v​v1vv_{1} is an edge, where recall that P:v1​v2P\colon v_{1}v_{2}. We note that vv and v2v_{2} may or may not be adjacent. Recall that k≤3k\leq 3, where kk denotes the number of components in G−MG-M.

Suppose that k=3k=3. In this case, if Dominator plays the vertex vv, then he marks both vertices in G1G_{1} and he marks at least one vertex in each of G2G_{2} and G3G_{3}, and therefore marks at least four vertices. Hence, Dominator can decrease the weight by at least 44, contradicting Claim 3.2.3. Therefore, k≤2k\leq 2. If k=1k=1, then n=4n=4, contradicting our earlier assumption that n≥6n\geq 6. Hence, k=2k=2.

If G2G_{2} has odd order, then GG would have odd order, contradicting the parity of nn (recall that n≥6n\geq 6 is even). Hence, G2G_{2} is either a P2P_{2}-component or a cycle component of even order. If G2G_{2} is a P2P_{2}-component, then n=6n=6. However if Dominator now plays the vertex vv, then he marks all four vertices in G1G_{1} and G2G_{2}, implying that the game is finished after Dominator’s first move, that is, after strictly less than 12​n\frac{1}{2}n moves, a contradiction. Hence, G2G_{2} is a cycle of even order. By Claim 3.2.5, no component in G−MG-M is a C4C_{4}-component. Hence, G2G_{2} is an even cycle of order at least 66. Let G2G_{2} be the cycle w1​w2​…​wq​w1w_{1}w_{2}\ldots w_{q}w_{1}, where q≥6q\geq 6 is an even integer.

Suppose that vv is adjacent to two or more vertices in G2G_{2}. In this case, as before if Dominator plays the vertex vv, then he decreases the weight by at least 44, a contradiction. Hence, vv is adjacent to exactly one vertex in G2G_{2}. Renaming vertices if necessary, we may assume that v​w1vw_{1} is an edge.

Suppose that q=6q=6, and so n=10n=10. In this case, Dominator plays as his first vertex the vertex vv, thereby marking the two vertices in G1G_{1} and the vertex w1w_{1} in G2G_{2}. Immediately after Dominator’s first move, we have M={u,v,v1,v2,w1}M=\{u,v,v_{1},v_{2},w_{1}\} and G−MG-M is a P5P_{5}-component given by w2​w3​w4​w5​w6w_{2}w_{3}w_{4}w_{5}w_{6}. If Staller now plays the vertex wiw_{i} on her second move for some i∈[6]i\in[6], then Dominator finishes the game by playing the vertex wi+3w_{i+3} where addition is taken modulo 66. Hence, the game is finished in four moves, and so ιg′​(G)≤4<12​n\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(G)\leq 4<\frac{1}{2}n (where recall that n=10n=10).

Thus, q≥8q\geq 8 and qq is even. In this case, Dominator plays as his first vertex the vertex w1w_{1}, thereby marking three new vertices in G2G_{2}, namely {w1,w2,wq}\{w_{1},w_{2},w_{q}\}. Thus at this stage of the game, we have M={u,v,w1,w2,wq}M=\{u,v,w_{1},w_{2},w_{q}\} and G−MG-M consists of two components, namely G1G_{1} and the path component G2′G_{2}^{\prime} given by w3​w4​…​wq−1w_{3}w_{4}\ldots w_{q-1}. We note that G2′G_{2}^{\prime} is a Pq−3P_{q-3}-component where q≥8q\geq 8.

Suppose that q≥12q\geq 12. In this case, whatever move Staller plays as her second move, with the updated set MM the graph G−MG-M contains a path component of order at least 44, contradicting Claim 3.2.4(d). Hence, q∈{8,10}q\in\{8,10\}. If q=8q=8, then n=12n=12, but in this case ιg′​(G)≤5<12​n\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(G)\leq 5<\frac{1}{2}n. If q=10q=10, then n=14n=14 and in this case ιg′​(G)≤6<12​n\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(G)\leq 6<\frac{1}{2}n. We therefore deduce that p=3p=3. This completes the proof of Claim 3.2.6. (□\Box)

By Claim 3.2.6, in the initial stage of the game when M={u,v}M=\{u,v\}, if G−MG-M contains a path component, then such a component is a P3P_{3}-component.

Claim 3.2.7.

In the initial stage of the game when M={u,v}M=\{u,v\}, if there exist at least two path components of G−MG-M, then G=F4G=F_{4}.

Proof.

Suppose that immediately after Staller’s first move, there exist two or more path components in G−MG-M. By Claim 3.2.6, every path component of G−MG-M is a P3P_{3}-component. Renaming the components of G−MG-M if necessary, we may assume that G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} are P3P_{3}-components. Suppose that k=3k=3. Since nn is even, the component G3G_{3} has even order, implying that G3G_{3} is a cycle of even order. By Claim 3.2.5, no component in G−MG-M is a C4C_{4}-component. Hence, G3G_{3} is an even cycle of order at least 66. Let G3G_{3} be the cycle w1​w2​…​wq​w1w_{1}w_{2}\ldots w_{q}w_{1}, where q≥6q\geq 6 is an even integer.

Let G1G_{1} be the path x1​x2​x3x_{1}x_{2}x_{3} and let G2G_{2} be the path y1​y2​y3y_{1}y_{2}y_{3}. If v​x2vx_{2} is an edge, then Dominator’s first move is vv, thereby marking all three vertices in G1G_{1} and at least one vertex in each of G2G_{2} and G3G_{3}. Hence in this case, Dominators marks at least five vertices, contradicting Claim 3.2.3. Hence, v​x2vx_{2} is not an edge. Renaming x1x_{1} and x3x_{3} if necessary, we may assume that v​x1∈E⁡(G)vx_{1}\in E(G). Analogously, we may assume that v​y1∈E⁡(G)vy_{1}\in E(G). Renaming vertices of G3G_{3} we may assume that v​w1∈E⁡(G)vw_{1}\in E(G).

Now Dominator’s first move is vv, thereby marking a vertex in each of G1G_{1}, G2G_{2} and G3G_{3}. In particular, we note that the vertex w1w_{1} is marked. q=6q=6.

Remark 3.3.

The inequalities of Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 hold true for arbitrary graphs, that is, they need not to be connected. This can be checked by observing that in the proofs of the inequalities, connectivity is not an issue.

4 The isolation game played in trees

As a consequence of Theorem 3.1, we have the following upper bound on the game isolation number of a tree.

Corollary 4.1.

If TT is a tree of order nn, then ιg​(T)≤12​n\iota_{\rm g}(T)\leq\frac{1}{2}n, with equality if and only if T=K2T=K_{2}.

In this section, we improve the 12​n\frac{1}{2}n-upper bound in Corollary 4.1 to a 511​n\frac{5}{11}n-upper bound when TT is a tree of order n≥3n\geq 3. For this purpose, we use a proof technique from Goddard and Henning (2025) used to establish upper bounds on the isolation number of a graph. The technique uses an isolation residual graph defined as follows.

Given a graph GG and a subset S⊆V⁡(G)S\subseteq V(G), the isolation residual graph denoted by GSιG_{S}^{\iota} is obtained as follows. Its vertex set is V⁡(G)V(G). Further:

  1. 1.

    A vertex in G−N⁡[S]G-N[S] with a neighbor in G−N⁡[S]G-N[S] is colored white.

  2. 2.

    A vertex in N⁡[S]N[S] with a white neighbor is colored blue.

  3. 3.

    All other vertices are colored red.

  4. 4.

    The edge set of GSιG_{S}^{\iota} consists of all edges of GG that are incident with at least one white vertex.

As remarked in Goddard and Henning (2025), the white vertices still need to be isolated, the blue vertices might be useful to do this isolating, and the red vertices are no longer relevant. We denote the set of red vertices by RR, the set of blue vertices by BB, and the set of white vertices by WW. We observe that these sets form a (weak) partition of V⁡(G)V(G). We shall need the following elementary properties of a residual graph.

Observation 4.2.

The following holds in the isolation residual graph GSιG_{S}^{\iota}.

  1. 1.

    Every vertex of SS is colored red.

  2. 2.

    Every red vertex is isolated, but no white nor blue vertex is isolated.

  3. 3.

    The degree of a white vertex in GSιG_{S}^{\iota} equals its degree in GG.

  4. 4.

    The set SS is an isolating set in GG if and only if there is no white vertex.

We are now in a position to prove the following result on the game isolation number of a tree.

Theorem 4.3.

If TT is a tree of order n≥3n\geq 3, then ιg​(T)≤511​n.\iota_{\rm g}(T)\leq\frac{5}{11}n.

Proof.

For a set S⊆V⁡(T)S\subseteq V(T), consider the isolation residual graph TSιT_{S}^{\iota} and the sets of white, blue, and red vertices in TSιT_{S}^{\iota}. We define the weight function

w⁡(TSι)=5​|W|+3​|B|.{\rm w}(T_{S}^{\iota})=5|W|+3|B|.

Equivalently, we associate every white, blue, and red vertex with a weight of 55, 33, and 00, respectively, and then consider the sum of the weights in GSιG_{S}^{\iota}.

When the game starts, S=∅S=\emptyset and w⁡(T∅ι)=5​n{\rm w}(T_{\emptyset}^{\iota})=5n, while w⁡(TSι)=0{\rm w}(T_{S}^{\iota})=0 holds when the game is over. Further, if vv is a playable vertex in the isolation residual graph TSιT_{S}^{\iota}, then w⁡(TSι)≥w⁡(TS∪{v}ι){\rm w}(T_{S}^{\iota})\geq{\rm w}(T_{S\cup\{v\}}^{\iota}) and we use the notation ξ⁡(v)=w⁡(TSι)−w⁡(TS∪{v}).\xi(v)={\rm w}(T_{S}^{\iota})-{\rm w}(T_{S\cup\{v\}}). We will show that Dominator can ensure that w⁡(TSι){\rm w}(T_{S}^{\iota}) decreases by at least 2222 in every two consecutive moves of Dominator and Staller. To prove this, we consider three stages in the D-game. In the graph TSι​[W]T_{S}^{\iota}[W], induced by the white vertices of TSιT_{S}^{\iota}, a big component is a component of order at least 44. If a component is not big, it is called small. If TT is a tree, a small component of TSι​[W]T_{S}^{\iota}[W] is either a P2P_{2}- or a P3P_{3}-subgraph.

Stage 11.

A move of Dominator belongs to Stage 11 if TSι​[W]T_{S}^{\iota}[W] contains a big component before this move. A move of Staller belongs to Stage 11, if so does Dominator’s previous move.

We first state that every legal move decreases w⁡(TSι){\rm w}(T_{S}^{\iota}) by at least 55. Indeed, if a white vertex vv is played, it becomes red and ξ⁡(v)≥5\xi(v)\geq 5. If a blue vertex uu is played that has a white neighbor u′u^{\prime}, then uu becomes red and u′u^{\prime} becomes blue or red, which gives ξ⁡(u)≥3+(5−3)=5.\xi(u)\geq 3+(5-3)=5. In particular, each move of Staller decreases the weight of TSιT_{S}^{\iota} by at least 55.

Suppose that Dominator plays in TSιT_{S}^{\iota} in Stage 11. The induced subgraph TSι​[W]T_{S}^{\iota}[W] then contains a component TiT_{i} on at least four vertices. If TiT_{i} is a star K1,kK_{1,k} for a k≥3k\geq 3, then Dominator chooses the center vv. Since all vertices in the star become red, ξ⁡(v)≥5​(k+1)≥20.\xi(v)\geq 5(k+1)\geq 20. If TiT_{i} is not a star, it contains a diametrical path v1​…​vdv_{1}\dots v_{d} with d≥4d\geq 4. Then P:v1​v2​v3​v4P\colon v_{1}v_{2}v_{3}v_{4} is a 44-path such that v1v_{1} is a leaf in TiT_{i} and if v2v_{2} has a neighbor v′∉V⁡(P)v^{\prime}\notin V(P), then v′v^{\prime} is a leaf in TiT_{i}. Dominator now plays v3v_{3}. With this move v1v_{1}, v2v_{2}, v3v_{3} (more generally, NTi​[v2]N_{T_{i}}[v_{2}]) become red and v4v_{4} is colored blue or red. Consequently, ξ⁡(v3)≥3×5+(5−3)=17.\xi(v_{3})\geq 3\times 5+(5-3)=17. This shows that Dominator can always decrease w⁡(TSι){\rm w}(T_{S}^{\iota}) by at least 1717, when the move belongs to Stage 11. We may conclude that Dominator has a strategy to ensure that the weight decreases by at least 17+5=2217+5=22 in every two consecutive moves in Stage 11.

Before discussing Stage 22, we introduce a new vertex type in the isolation residual graph TSιT_{S}^{\iota}. We say that a vertex uu is light blue, and belongs to BℓB^{\ell}, if it became blue during Stage 22. Light blue vertices are associated with a weight of 11; that is, the new weight function we use in Stages 22 and 33 is

w⁡(TSι)=5​|W|+3​|B∖Bℓ|+|Bℓ|.{\rm w}(T_{S}^{\iota})=5|W|+3|B\setminus B^{\ell}|+|B^{\ell}|.

Note that all light blue vertices are of degree 11. Further, we say that a component TiT_{i} of TSι​[W]T_{S}^{\iota}[W] is special, if it is a P2P_{2}-component and each adjacent blue (or light blue) vertex is of degree 11 in TSιT_{S}^{\iota}.

Stage 2.

A move of Dominator belongs to Stage 22, if the subgraph TSι​[W]T_{S}^{\iota}[W] in TSιT_{S}^{\iota} before this move consists only of small components and not all of them are special. A move of Staller belongs to Stage 22, if so does Dominator’s previous move.

We first prove that every move vv of Staller decreases w⁡(TSι){\rm w}(T_{S}^{\iota}) by at least 77 in Stage 22. If vv is a white vertex, then an entire P2P_{2}- or P3P_{3}-component of G⁡[W]G[W] becomes red and ξ⁡(v)≥2×5=10.\xi(v)\geq 2\times 5=10. The same is true if v∈Bv\in B and a white neighbor v′v^{\prime} belongs to a P2P_{2}-component. Assume v∈Bv\in B and that a neighbor v′v^{\prime} of vv is from a P3P_{3}-component of TSι​[W]T_{S}^{\iota}[W]. We remark that in this case v∈B∖Bℓv\in B\setminus B^{\ell} because there were no components in TSι​[W]T_{S}^{\iota}[W] on more than three vertices at the beginning of Stage 22, and so vv was not white at that time. If v′v^{\prime} is the central vertex of the P3P_{3}-component, then v′v^{\prime} and the entire P3P_{3}-component becomes red with this move and we have ξ⁡(v)≥3+3×5=18.\xi(v)\geq 3+3\times 5=18. If v′v^{\prime} is a leaf in the P3P_{3}-component, then vv becomes red and v′v^{\prime} becomes light blue with this move. Therefore, ξ⁡(v)≥3+(5−1)=7,\xi(v)\geq 3+(5-1)=7, completing the proof of the statement.

Consider now Dominator’s move. If a P3P_{3}-component is present in TSι​[W]T_{S}^{\iota}[W], he can choose a vertex vv from such a component TiT_{i}. All three white vertices of TiT_{i} become red, which results in ξ⁡(v)≥3×5=15.\xi(v)\geq 3\times 5=15. If there is no P3P_{3}-component, then a non-special P2P_{2}-component exists. Dominator may choose a blue vertex uu that has neighbors u1u_{1} and u2u_{2} from two different P2P_{2}-components. Playing uu, both components and uu itself become red and ξ⁡(u)≥4×5+3=23.\xi(u)\geq 4\times 5+3=23. We may conclude that Dominator is always able to decrease w⁡(TSι){\rm w}(T_{S}^{\iota}) by at least 1515 with a move in Stage 22 and therefore, every two consecutive moves together decrease the weight of the isolation residual graph by at least 7+15=227+15=22.

Stage 33.

Stage 33 starts when all components of TSι​[W]T_{S}^{\iota}[W] are special and ends when the game is over.

Each move of a player removes a P2P_{2}-component from TSιT_{S}^{\iota} by recoloring both vertices with red. Further, by Observation 4.2(c) and the condition n≥3n\geq 3 in the theorem, each special component is adjacent to a blue vertex of degree 11, which also becomes red together with the component. We infer that w⁡(TSι){\rm w}(T_{S}^{\iota}) decreases by at least 2×5+1=112\times 5+1=11 with each move played in Stage 33, no matter whether the move is played by Dominator or by Staller.

By the analysis of the stages of the game when Dominator follows the described strategy, we obtained that, on average, each move decreases w⁡(TSι){\rm w}(T_{S}^{\iota}) by at least 1111. Let tt denote the number of vertices played in the game. As the game started with w⁡(T∅ι)=5​n{\rm w}(T_{\emptyset}^{\iota})=5n and finished with w⁡(TSι)=0{\rm w}(T_{S}^{\iota})=0, we conclude 11​t≤5​n11t\leq 5n and then, ιg​(T)≤t≤511​n\iota_{\rm g}(T)\leq t\leq\frac{5}{11}n follows. ∎

5 On the 3/7-bound

Brešar et al. (2026) posed the following conjecture.

Conjecture 5.1.

For any graph GG with no K2K_{2}-components,

ιg​(G)≤⌈37​n​(G)⌉​ and ​ιg′​(G)≤⌈37​n​(G)⌉.\iota_{\rm g}(G)\leq\left\lceil\frac{3}{7}n(G)\right\rceil\text{ and }\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(G)\leq\left\lceil\frac{3}{7}n(G)\right\rceil.

If the conjecture holds true, then it is sharp as the following example from Brešar et al. (2026) demonstrates. Start with an arbitrary graph GG and attach to each vertex of it two disjoint paths of length three. Besides this family of graphs and graphs similar to them (say, obtained from such a graph by removing a pendant vertex), the authors could not find any other infinite family of graphs whose game isolation number is close to 3​n​(G)/73n(G)/7. Here, we present another such family.

If GG is a graph, then let G^\widehat{G} be a graph defined as follows. For any vertex v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G), add two disjoint triangles TvT_{v} and Tv′T_{v}^{\prime}, and add an edge between vv and a vertex of TvT_{v} and an edge between vv and a vertex of Tv′T_{v}^{\prime}, see Fig. 2.

Proposition 5.2.

If GG is a graph, then

ιg​(G^)=ιg′​(G^)=37​n​(G^).\iota_{\rm g}(\widehat{G})=\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(\widehat{G})=\frac{3}{7}n(\widehat{G})\,.
Proof.

For a vertex v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G), let GvG_{v} be the subgraph of G^\widehat{G} induced by {v}∪V⁡(Tv)∪V⁡(Tv′),\{v\}\cup V(T_{v})\cup V(T_{v}^{\prime}), see Fig. 2 again.

Consider the following strategy of Dominator that guarantees that not more than three vertices are played in each GvG_{v}. Assume that the last move of Staller is a vertex from GvG_{v}, for some v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G). If there are vertices of GvG_{v} which remain playable, then Dominator plays a vertex of GvG_{v} such that no more than three vertices from GvG_{v} will be played when the game finishes. He can achieve this goal since if Staller played vv, then Dominator selects a vertex from TvT_{v} or a vertex from Tv′T_{v}^{\prime}, and if Staller selects some vertex from V⁡(Tv)∪V⁡(Tv′)V(T_{v})\cup V(T_{v}^{\prime}), then Dominator replies by playing vv if possible, otherwise a vertex from the triangle where no vertex has been played yet. Note that Dominator can also follow this strategy for his first move in the D-game, that is, he selects some vertex v∈V⁡(G)⊆V⁡(G^)v\in V(G)\subseteq V(\widehat{G}). On the other hand, if no vertex of GvG_{v} remains playable after the last move of Staller, Dominator applies analogous strategy in some GuG_{u}, u≠vu\neq v, where there still exist playable vertices. Note that this strategy of Dominator can be applied no matter whether the D-game or the S-game is played. We can conclude that ιg​(G^)≤37​n​(G^)\iota_{\rm g}(\widehat{G})\leq\frac{3}{7}n(\widehat{G}) as well as ιg′​(G^)≤37​n​(G^).\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(\widehat{G})\leq\frac{3}{7}n(\widehat{G}).

Consider now the following strategy of Staller. Her goal is that in each GvG_{v}, the vertex vv is selected during the game, either by Dominator or by Staller. So assume that the last move of Dominator is a vertex from GvG_{v}, for some v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G), and that no other vertex of GvG_{v} has yet been played. If Dominator selected vv, then Staller replies by selecting a neighbor of vv in TvT_{v}. On the other hand, if Dominator selected a vertex different from vv, then Staller selects vv. In either case, this strategy of Staller guarantees that by the end of the game, three vertices from GvG_{v} are selected. In addition, if Staller is forced to play first on some GvG_{v}, then she selects vv, thus forcing again that three vertices from GvG_{v} will be played. We can conclude that ιg​(G^)≥37​n​(G^)\iota_{\rm g}(\widehat{G})\geq\frac{3}{7}n(\widehat{G}) as well as ιg′​(G^)≥37​n​(G^),\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(\widehat{G})\geq\frac{3}{7}n(\widehat{G}), and we are done. ∎

Both the previously known extremal family (based on attaching two paths of length three) and our construction (based on attaching two triangles) share a common structural feature. Each vertex of the original graph is extended into a local configuration on seven vertices that requires at least three vertices in any optimal isolating set. Consequently, these constructions can be viewed as decomposing the graph into disjoint 7-vertex gadgets contributing exactly 3 to the game isolation number, which explains the emergence of the 37\frac{3}{7} ratio. This suggests that the conjectured upper bound is driven by such local configurations, rather than global properties of the graph, and that extremal graphs may be characterized by the presence of these forcing gadgets.

We conclude the paper with the following slight refinements of Conjecture 5.1.

Conjecture 5.3.

If GG is a graph of order nn with δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2, then ιg​(G)≤37​n\iota_{\rm g}(G)\leq\frac{3}{7}n and ιg′​(G)≤37​n\iota_{\rm g}^{\prime}(G)\leq\frac{3}{7}n.

If Conjecture 5.3 is correct, then we have seen above that it is tight and achievable for connected graphs GG of arbitrarily large order.

Conjecture 5.4.

If TT is a tree of order n≥3n\geq 3, then ιg​(T)≤37​n\iota_{\rm g}(T)\leq\frac{3}{7}n.
